haiku-low.q1: A person starts it with the failover command. Detection only pages on-call when 2 of 3 probes see 3 failures. It takes no automatic action.
haiku-low.q2: The command stops with nothing changed, unless an explicit accept-data-loss override flag is given. With the override, it proceeds.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion: the fence wait has finished (A's lease expiry plus margin). Before B's workers start: B's database is writable. Before DNS moves: B's app is scaled to 12, passing health, and workers are running.
haiku-low.q4: Sessions live in each region's Redis, which is not replicated. Users signed in at failover time must sign in again on B.
haiku-low.q5: It is never reused as primary. It is rebuilt as a replica of B via fresh base backup or pg_rewind. Moving back to A needs a separate planned switchover.
haiku-low.q6: A's watchdog stops A's database about 15 s after its last successful lease renewal. The command's FAILING_OVER write blocks renewal, and it waits for lease expiry plus margin before promoting B.
haiku-low.q7: A strongly consistent record store outside both regions holds it. The failover command reads and writes the record; the watchdog renews a separate lease key in that store; DNS is changed only after the record says B.
haiku-low.q8: Before workers start, the command resets every running job row to queued on B. Jobs may therefore run twice, so handlers must be idempotent with idempotency keys.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command with --resume from any host after confirming the earlier run is stopped; it continues from the recorded step. Going back to A after the FAILING_OVER write is a manual human decision.
haiku-low.q10: A's users get errors until DNS moves, since A's database is stopped. Resolvers may serve A's address for up to 60 s after the DNS change. The document does not say more.
haiku-low.q11: Target RPO is 30 s. Writes after A's last WAL receipt are lost. The replay lag check of 30 s or less does not guarantee RPO; the command prints the last WAL receipt time.

sonnet.q1: Only a person starts a failover, by running the failover command (RTO clock starts then). Detection (probes: 2 of 3 locations see 3 consecutive /healthz failures, every 10 s) only pages on-call; no automatic action.
sonnet.q2: Pre-checks stop the command with nothing changed if B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s, unless an explicit accept-data-loss override flag (e.g. --accept-data-loss) is given; with the override it proceeds.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B's DB: record written as FAILING_OVER (epoch +1, compare-and-set), best-effort stop of A, and the fence wait (A's lease expiry plus clock-skew margin) finished. Before B's workers start: B's database is promoted and writable, and running jobs requeued (step 7 before workers). Before DNS moves: DB writable, B app scaled to 12 and passing /healthz with all 12 healthy, and B's workers group running at full desired count.
sonnet.q4: Sessions are lost: Redis is per-region and not replicated, B's Redis starts empty, so users signed in at failover time must sign in again on B. Accepted, no step.
sonnet.q5: It stays stopped (lease expired, record says B active with higher epoch, watchdog can't renew). It is never reused as primary; rebuild it as a replica of B via fresh base backup or pg_rewind. Moving back to A is a separate planned switchover; no automatic failback.
sonnet.q6: The write lease and watchdog on A's primary host: A may take writes only while it keeps renewing the lease; the FAILING_OVER record write makes renewal impossible (or store unreachable also fails renewal), so about 15 s after last successful renewal the watchdog fast-shuts-down A's PostgreSQL. The command waits for lease expiry plus margin before promoting B. Residual risk: frozen/paused watchdog or excessive clock skew.
sonnet.q7: The active-region record in a strongly consistent store outside both regions (third location/provider; compare-and-set and multi-key transactions). The failover command reads it (pre-checks, resume) and writes it (FAILING_OVER, step, ACTIVE). A's watchdog reads it as part of each lease-renewal transaction (extends the separate lease key only if record still says A active with its epoch). Not stated: any other readers; DNS is not the source of truth.
sonnet.q8: B's jobs table shows them as running (as of last WAL received) but workers are gone. Before any worker starts, the command resets all running rows to queued (idempotent), so they re-run on B. Jobs may therefore run twice (side effects already done in A), so handlers must be idempotent/use idempotency keys. Jobs A enqueued or committed after the last WAL receipt are not on B and cannot be listed; the command prints a summary of this.
sonnet.q9: Retry the failing step about 3 times, then exit with an error naming the step; on-call calls the secondary, and after the fix confirms the earlier command isn't running and reruns with --resume (from any host), which takes run_id from the record and continues from the recorded step, with real state overriding the step field. Going back to A: only before the FAILING_OVER write (a stop changes nothing, just start again later). After it, backing out is a manual human decision because A has stopped itself and needs un-fencing; otherwise resume forward.
sonnet.q10: Resolvers may serve A's address for up to 60 s (TTL) after DNS moves. During the failover A's app tier stays up but gets database errors once A's DB is stopped (about 15 s after fencing begins), so such clients see errors until DNS moves/cache expires, then reach B and must sign in again. Not stated beyond that.
sonnet.q11: Asynchronous replication, so writes A committed after B's last WAL receipt are lost. Target RPO is 30 s, enforced only by the pre-check that B's recorded replay lag (typically under 5 s) is 30 s or less, which can be overridden. The check does not guarantee RPO: the recorded lag doesn't grow while A is down and says nothing about later commits; the command prints the last WAL receipt time so on-call can judge the gap.
